I disagree about Java but I do agree that NodeJS and others are the future and if you want to do backend development it pays to know these things. You need to preface this stuff with "depending on location" and "startups don't use java" and "many companies doing brand new stuff don't use Java". You are speaking mainly to the coast where maybe Java isn't as widely used, but in other areas of the country, it's very prevalent. I personally prefer full stack JS becauseI love React, and Node, serverless / lambdas, etc. are fun to develop with, more flexible and I think the community around them is stronger for the future. The reason I want to focus on Java here for a second is for the people who are looking for a foot in the door to the industry - don't write it off immediately. Pragmatism is your friend. Evidence can be seen that Java still has a huge representation in the USA overall. if you look at the Stack Overflow statistics - Java still represents in the Top 5 languages for respondents, but is lower on the "wanted" technology. To me this is indicative of the fact that many companies still have Java, and from what I have seen most of them WANT to move into other backend technology, however, it's obviously a slower moving process to get off of Java. Many companies I have seen in the Midwest that aren't a .NET shop have Java development positions that allow people a path to help move the technology forward over time as they develop their career. There are lots of opportunities to get started in software development with Java to get a foot in the door at a company if you aren't someone who demands to work in the valley. Often these doors will allow you to grow into those newer technologies and for the strong players, it will lead them towards the more senior roles, or architect roles because they will become known as the movers and shakers who helped take the company into its next 5-7 year lifecycle of new languages. I like the idea behind this video because I think you are helping to educate people on several levels. I run a consulting company and as such I interview a lot of people. Many resumes are bloated with buzzwords of technologies written by people who haven't identified what they want to be or do in their career - the tech list is way too broad, it's literally impossible to be an expert in everything. But you will see people who are not figuring out their career path and tailoring their resume and experience to following that. Career path is part of a broader plan for your life and people need to spend more time thinking about what they want to do and the prospects. Another great TechLead video by the tech lead.
